education.label: 教育
education.title: Learning to Ask Better Questions
education.essay:
Most classrooms reward the student with the fastest answer. Yet the habit that carries people through adult life is not answering quickly; it is asking precisely. A good question turns a vague curiosity into a manageable problem, and it gives other people a reason to think alongside us.

In my first year of university, I spent weeks reading about urban gardens without knowing what I wanted to find out. My notes grew longer while my understanding stayed flat. A tutor finally asked me to write one sentence beginning with “I want to know whether…” The exercise felt almost childish, but it exposed the emptiness at the centre of my reading. Once the sentence existed, I could sort sources, reject irrelevant claims and design a small interview.

Better questions also make disagreement less expensive. Instead of announcing that someone is wrong, we can ask which evidence would change their mind. This shifts the conversation from defending a position to examining it, and it often reveals that two people are answering different questions.

Schools could teach this deliberately. Give students five minutes to write three questions about a text, then ask them to choose the one they cannot answer alone. The room becomes quieter, but the thinking becomes louder. Answers may finish a lesson; questions decide what the lesson is for.

technology.label: 科技
technology.title: The Quiet Cost of Convenience
technology.essay:
A map application can now tell me where to turn before I have looked at the street. This is convenient, and that is precisely the problem. Convenience hides its costs by removing friction, and friction is often where attention, memory and judgement are built.

Consider navigation. When I walked through a new city with a paper map, I made wrong turns and remembered their causes. A phone guides me perfectly and leaves almost nothing behind. The destination arrives, but the route does not become part of my mental map. The same pattern appears in note-taking and translation tools: the smoother the output, the easier it is to mistake delivery for understanding.

This is not an argument for abandoning useful technology. It is an argument for choosing where to keep a little difficulty. A student might draft an answer before consulting a chatbot. A traveller might study the route for one minute before pressing start. Such habits preserve the small struggle that turns information into knowledge.

Designers can help by making the cost visible: a quiet summary of what a tool did, a prompt to recall before revealing, a record of decisions the user delegated. Convenience is not the enemy. Passive convenience is. The best tools should leave us more capable after use, not merely more comfortable during it.

environment.label: 环境
environment.title: The City That Learned to Breathe
environment.essay:
For decades, the river through my hometown was treated as a drain. Concrete walls kept it out of sight, and the city turned its back on the water. Then a modest experiment began: one section of the embankment was replaced with reeds, shallow pools and a narrow walking path. Nobody expected much. Within three years, herons returned.

The project succeeded because it was small enough to be tested and visible enough to be defended. Residents could see the change on their way to work. Children counted insects for a school project. The data mattered, but the daily encounter mattered more. Environmental policy often fails not because the science is weak, but because the benefits remain abstract until people can touch them.

There were costs. Maintenance was more demanding than concrete, and some paths flooded after heavy rain. The city did not hide these problems; it published them alongside the results. That honesty made the next stage easier to fund.

Cities cannot be returned to some imagined untouched nature. They can, however, make room for other lives in ordinary places. A reed bed beside a bus stop will not stop climate change, but it changes what a city believes it is for. Once residents see the river as a neighbour rather than a drain, better decisions become possible.

society.label: 社会
society.title: The Neighbour Nobody Noticed
society.essay:
Mr Lin repaired bicycles in a narrow shop at the end of our street. He was not a community leader. He never spoke at meetings. Yet when the shop closed, the street discovered how much invisible work he had been doing. He had watched children cross the road, lent tools, kept spare keys and told newcomers which bus to take.

Cities tend to count what is easy to count: shops, jobs, square metres. Informal care is harder to measure, so it disappears from planning documents. A bench is just a bench until you notice who rests there. A corner shop is a business until it becomes the place where an elderly resident hears a daily greeting.

Recognising this work is not nostalgia. It affects policy. If a redevelopment plan removes small, low-rent spaces, it may also remove the conditions for casual contact. Planners can ask a simple question before approving a project: where will the unplanned conversations happen afterwards?

Mr Lin now works from a folding table near the bus stop. People still stop to talk. The street has not preserved his shop, but it has learned to see the role. That may be the beginning of a better kind of urban knowledge: not only how many people live here, but how they look after one another.

culture.label: 文化
culture.title: A Recipe Is a Small Archive
culture.essay:
My grandmother never wrote down her dumpling recipe. She measured flour by feel and judged the filling by smell. When she died, the recipe did not disappear completely, but it became a set of questions that only she could answer.

Cooking is often treated as a private skill. In fact, it carries public memory. A recipe records what a place grew, what it could afford and whom it traded with. The use of a particular pickle or a forbidden ingredient can tell a longer story than a history book. When families move, recipes travel with them and change. The changes are not mistakes; they are evidence.

This is why I began writing down not only quantities but reasons. Why is the dough rested twice? Which step can be skipped when there is no time? What should the kitchen smell like? A useful recipe preserves decisions, not just ingredients.

My version will never taste exactly like hers. I have a different flour, a different stove and a smaller kitchen. Still, when I fold the dough, I am repeating a gesture that arrived before me. The archive is not on paper. It is in the hands, and it survives each time someone bothers to cook.

growth.label: 个人成长
growth.title: The Year I Practised Being Slow
growth.essay:
I used to treat speed as proof of seriousness. A full calendar meant I mattered. I answered messages while walking, read summaries instead of books and felt guilty during any pause. Then a minor illness forced me to spend two weeks doing almost nothing.

The first days were unbearable. Without constant input, I noticed how much of my busyness was avoidance. Being slow exposed thoughts I had been outrunning: a difficult conversation, a project I did not believe in, the fear that I had chosen the wrong direction.

Recovery did not turn me into a calm person. It gave me a smaller, more practical idea: slowness is a tool, not an identity. I now protect one unhurried hour each morning. I write before opening my inbox. Once a week, I walk without headphones. These are modest rules, but they make room for attention.

The lesson was not that busy people are shallow or that slowness is virtuous. It was that pace should match purpose. Some tasks deserve urgency; others need the patience to become clear. Choosing the right speed is part of the work itself.
